paragraphs: Anomaly detection methods try to identify unusual observations, but their usefulness depends on the conditions in which they are tested. ADBench organizes evaluation around three practical questions: how performance changes with available supervision, with the kind of anomaly being detected, and with noise or corruption in the data.

The contribution is a broad comparison framework covering 30 algorithms and 57 datasets. Across 98,436 experiments, the researchers examine these conditions systematically. The benchmark also includes contributed datasets from language and vision, expanding the settings in which researchers can compare a new detector with existing approaches.

The reported findings identify meaningful patterns concerning supervision and anomaly types, with implications for choosing and designing algorithms. The abstract does not name a single winning detector; its stated contribution is the comparative evidence and evaluation infrastructure. By releasing both the benchmark and its results, the authors make comprehensive comparisons easier to reproduce and give researchers a shared basis for assessing future methods.
neurips-2022-adbench-anomaly-detection-b.tldr: ADBench compares 30 anomaly detection algorithms across 57 datasets to examine how supervision, anomaly types, and corrupted data affect performance.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition compresses multidimensional data into simpler components that can also help interpret its features. However, accurately fitting the original measurements is not necessarily the same as preserving what a classifier needs. Raw signals can contain irrelevant information, so a reconstruction-focused objective may spend capacity representing details unrelated to the eventual classification task.

Augmented Tensor Decomposition, or ATD, incorporates data augmentation and self-supervised learning into the decomposition objective. The approach uses these additional learning signals to improve the usefulness of the resulting features for classification. Because the augmented objective is non-convex, the authors develop an iterative optimization method that follows the alternating least squares style used in tensor decomposition.

Across multiple datasets, ATD reports accuracy gains of 0.8%–2.5% over tensor-based baselines. Against self-supervised and autoencoder baselines, it achieves comparable or better performance, with improvements reaching 15% in accuracy while using less than 5% of their learnable parameters. These findings support changing the decomposition objective to favor classification-relevant structure while retaining a compact model.
neurips-2022-atd-augmenting-cp-tensor-de.tldr: ATD adds augmentation and self-supervised learning to tensor decomposition, improving downstream classification with relatively few learnable parameters.

paragraphs: Users can pool information to estimate the distributions generating their data, but communication limits restrict how much they can share. Existing efficient methods often assume everyone samples from the same discrete distribution. This paper studies a more flexible setting in which users differ, while their distributions vary on only a small number of entries.

The proposed SHIFT method separates collaboration from personalization. First, users communicate with a server to estimate a central distribution using robust statistical methods. Then that shared estimate is fine-tuned to recover each user's individual distribution. This organization lets users benefit from common information while allowing the sparse differences specified by the model.

The authors prove minimax optimality under their heterogeneity model and communication constraints: the method achieves the best worst-case estimation performance characterized by that setting. The sparse-variation assumption is therefore part of the guarantee, rather than an incidental detail. Experiments with synthetic data and text n-gram frequencies corroborate the method's efficiency and illustrate its use for estimating differing distributions collaboratively.
neurips-2022-collaborative-learning-of-d.tldr: SHIFT combines robust shared estimation with individual fine-tuning to optimally learn sparsely differing discrete distributions under communication constraints.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means using familiar task elements in new combinations. This paper investigates how that ability appears in human behavior and brain activity, and whether a corresponding ability can be developed in artificial neural networks. The researchers use a highly compositional task and whole-cortex fMRI measurements to connect behavioral patterns with neural representations.

For the artificial networks, the authors introduce primitives pretraining: training procedures that supply prior knowledge of the task's component elements. Networks receiving this preparation show greater correspondence with both human behavior and neural signatures of composition. They also develop abstract internal representations, generalize well without training on the new combinations, and learn efficiently from examples.

The resulting representations form a hierarchy that matches patterns in the human fMRI data. Abstractions of sensory rules correspond to earlier sensory areas, while abstractions of motor rules correspond to later motor areas. These empirical findings support abstract representations as a possible neural implementation of compositional generalization and show how targeted pretraining can encourage related representations in artificial networks.
neurips-2022-compositional-generalizatio.tldr: Pretraining networks on task primitives produces abstract representations and compositional generalization that correspond with human behavior and brain activity.

paragraphs: This paper develops private learning algorithms whose guarantees depend on prediction margins without depending on input dimension. A margin captures how confidently a model separates its predictions. Connecting privacy guarantees with margin-based learning provides a way to characterize performance that does not automatically worsen merely because the input has more coordinates.

For linear models, the authors provide a pure differentially private algorithm with relative-deviation margin guarantees, alongside an efficient private algorithm with margin guarantees. They also develop an efficient method for kernel models using shift-invariant kernels, including Gaussian kernels, and describe extensions to other kernels through oblivious sketching. A further pure-private algorithm covers a family of feed-forward neural networks.

The paper additionally treats label privacy through a general algorithm applicable to broad hypothesis families, including neural networks. Finally, it explains how to add model selection to the private learning procedures to choose a confidence-margin parameter. The contribution spans several model classes and privacy formulations; the abstract distinguishes pure privacy, computational efficiency, and label privacy rather than assigning every property to every algorithm.
neurips-2022-differentially-private-lear.tldr: The paper develops private learning algorithms with dimension-independent margin guarantees for linear models, kernel models, and a family of neural networks.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may encounter changes in how its environment behaves or in what it is rewarded for doing. Representing all such changes with one shared vector can obscure their separate influences. FANS-RL instead models non-stationarity through individual hidden change factors and causal relationships across environments.

The method jointly learns a factored representation of the decision process and representations of the time-varying factors. Under the paper's stated standard assumptions, the authors prove complete recovery of the causal graph describing factored transitions and rewards. They also establish recovery of a partial structure linking individual change factors to state components; that second recovery claim is explicitly more limited.

The framework accommodates different kinds and frequencies of change, including changes between episodes and during an episode. Experiments report better returns, more compact latent state representations, and greater robustness to differing degrees of non-stationarity than existing approaches. Together, the theory and experiments support separating sources of change as a useful way to adapt, while the structural recovery guarantee remains conditional on its assumptions.
neurips-2022-factored-adaptation-for-non.tldr: FANS-RL learns separate hidden change factors and causal structure to improve adaptation when reinforcement learning environments or rewards change.

paragraphs: Self-paced learning controls the progression of training through a regularizer and a gradually increasing parameter called age. Choosing where to stop this progression is difficult. One way to understand the choice is to trace the age-path: the sequence of learned solutions obtained as the age parameter changes over a range.

GAGA provides a path-following algorithm for various self-paced regularizers. It combines ordinary differential equations with set control to track the solution across age values. This broadens the scope beyond earlier algorithms that were restricted to the simplest regularizer or lacked a strong combination of theoretical understanding and computational efficiency.

The authors describe GAGA as, to their knowledge, the first exact age-path algorithm for general self-paced regularizers. They give concrete algorithmic steps for support vector machines and Lasso, and report considerable speedups over competing baselines on real-world datasets. Computing the path makes the effect of the age parameter accessible across a range; the stated contribution is this exact and efficient tracking, rather than a claimed universal stopping rule.
neurips-2022-gaga-deciphering-age-path-o.tldr: GAGA uses differential equations and set control to efficiently trace exact solution paths across age parameters for general self-paced regularizers.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks use neuron models that accumulate inputs and produce spikes. The widely used leaky integrate-and-fire formulation has many variants, but the paper argues that most support only one biological feature within a given neuronal behavior. That restriction limits the range of dynamics the neurons can express.

GLIF combines multiple biological features within a unified neuron formulation. Learnable gates determine the proportions in which those features contribute. Together with other trainable membrane-related parameters, these gates let neurons develop different behaviors and adapt during training. The architectural change therefore expands the representation available at the level of the individual spiking neuron.

Across several datasets, the authors report improved performance over other spiking networks by replacing their neuron formulations with GLIF. A spiking ResNet-19 using GLIF reaches 77.35% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 with six time steps, reported as advancing the state of the art. These results support the value of richer, learnable neuronal dynamics; the abstract's energy-efficiency motivation is separate from these reported accuracy findings.
neurips-2022-glif-a-unified-gated-leaky-.tldr: GLIF uses learnable gates to combine biological neuron features, increasing spiking-network flexibility and improving reported classification performance.

paragraphs: Distance fields describe a three-dimensional surface through values assigned to locations in space. Signed distance approaches support high-quality reconstruction but, in the setting described here, represent closed shapes. Unsigned distance approaches can also handle open surfaces, yet converting their signless output into high-quality polygon meshes introduces an additional challenge.

HSDF combines an unsigned distance prediction with a separately learned sign field produced by a classifier. This hybrid representation supports both open and closed surfaces while remaining compatible with existing iso-surface extraction techniques. The method first generates surface points to locate the relevant surface, then uses adaptive meshing to create polygons only in regions containing it.

The authors also introduce HSDF-Net, which separates learning the hybrid representation into two easier problems. Experiments across multiple datasets report qualitative and quantitative improvements over state-of-the-art techniques. The contribution links two practical needs: representing surfaces with varied topology and converting that representation into a mesh. Learning sign information separately and restricting mesh construction to surface-containing regions are central to connecting those needs.
neurips-2022-hsdf-hybrid-sign-and-distan.tldr: HSDF combines unsigned distances, a learned sign field, and adaptive meshing to reconstruct both open and closed surfaces as polygon meshes.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search makes choosing network operations manageable by replacing discrete choices with continuously adjustable magnitudes. Gradient descent can optimize those magnitudes efficiently, but a separate question remains: which operations should become part of the final network? Standard DARTS treats larger optimized magnitudes as evidence that an operation matters more.

This paper examines that selection step using influence functions and Taylor expansions. It approximates how a candidate operation influences the supernet, the network containing the candidate operations during search. The analysis shows that operation strength depends on second-order information as well as magnitude. The resulting selection criterion, Influential Magnitude, incorporates this richer account of an operation's effect.

The distinction matters because optimizing a continuous search representation does not itself establish that magnitude ranks operations correctly. The authors give a theoretical basis for changing that ranking rule. Across several search spaces and tasks, their experiments show that DARTS and its variants can avoid most failures using the proposed criterion. This is an empirical improvement across the tested settings, not a claim that all architecture-search failures disappear.
neurips-2022-interpreting-operation-sele.tldr: Influential Magnitude uses operation magnitudes and second-order information to improve the final operation choices made by differentiable architecture search.

paragraphs: Inverse game theory starts with observed strategic behavior and asks what underlying preferences could have produced it. This paper studies that question for Stackelberg games, which involve a leader and a follower. Earlier results found statistical and computational difficulties when the follower was assumed to behave with perfect rationality.

The authors replace perfect rationality with the classic quantal response model of bounded rationality. Under this model, the follower's behavior has a smooth dependence on utility. The paper shows that this smoothness makes the follower's utility parameters provably more efficient to learn in general Stackelberg games. A less idealized behavioral assumption therefore makes this inference problem more tractable.

Experiments on synthesized games confirm the theoretical results and suggest robustness even when behavior does not strictly follow the quantal response model. Those two conclusions have different strengths: efficient learning is proved under the modeled behavior, while performance beyond that model is supported empirically. The central finding is that bounded rationality can supply useful structure for recovering preferences from strategic observations.
neurips-2022-inverse-game-theory-for-sta.tldr: Modeling followers with quantal-response bounded rationality makes their utility parameters provably easier to learn in Stackelberg games.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves integer programming problems by exploring portions of a search space. Its node-comparison rule determines which portion to investigate next, so that ordering influences how the search proceeds. This paper learns the comparison rule with a graph neural network, using structured representations of the candidate search nodes.

Each search node is represented as a bipartite graph carrying attributes. A siamese graph neural network compares these representations, and training imitates a diving oracle that heads toward an optimal solution. The learned comparisons then determine node ranks in a plain evaluation framework where exploration follows that ranking.

On three NP-hard benchmarks selected to be particularly difficult for finding feasible solutions, the method solves instances faster and produces smaller search trees than SCIP's default ranking rule and competing machine learning approaches. The reported advantages also extend to instances larger than those used in training. These results support learned graph-based comparisons as a way to improve search ordering in the tested setting, including beyond the training instance sizes.
neurips-2022-learning-to-compare-nodes-i.tldr: A siamese graph neural network learns branch-and-bound node rankings that yield faster solving and smaller search trees on three challenging benchmarks.

paragraphs: Measurements from connected sensors can be represented as signals changing over a graph. When several sensors have long, overlapping gaps, reconstructing those signals becomes difficult. Autoregressive models process sequences recursively, and the paper identifies brittleness and unstable learning as problems when the observations are highly sparse.

The proposed attention-based architectures reconstruct missing values by conditioning only on available observations. A spatiotemporal propagation architecture learns representations for particular locations and times, with its organization aligned to the imputation task. Training is end-to-end and reconstructs observations in relation to the corresponding sensor and its neighboring graph nodes.

This design handles sparse observations without propagating prediction errors through the reconstruction process. It also captures dependencies in both temporal directions without requiring a bidirectional model. Experiments on representative benchmarks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The key contribution is a reconstruction strategy organized around the observed evidence across space and time, addressing the difficulties that arise when recursive sequence processing must cope with extensive missing data.
neurips-2022-learning-to-reconstruct-mis.tldr: An attention-based spatiotemporal graph model reconstructs missing measurements from available observations without propagating prediction errors.

paragraphs: Solving partial differential equations at finer spatial and temporal resolutions can become extremely expensive. The paper motivates this problem through fluid simulation and climate prediction, where coarse grids can miss important turbulent behavior. MAgNet approaches the computational challenge with a learned representation that predicts a solution at a queried spatial position.

The architecture combines an implicit neural representation with a graph neural network. Its coordinate-based component represents the solution continuously in space, while the graph-based component supports working with meshes. This combination enables prediction on previously unseen non-uniform meshes without additional training, connecting continuous spatial queries with data represented on discrete simulation points.

Across several PDE simulation datasets, MAgNet produces accurate predictions and compares favorably with existing baselines. The authors report physically consistent predictions up to 250 frames ahead and generalization to meshes and resolutions up to four times those used for training. These findings support flexibility across discretizations in the evaluated simulations; the climate discussion provides motivation rather than a reported climate forecasting deployment.
neurips-2022-magnet-mesh-agnostic-neural.tldr: MAgNet combines continuous coordinate-based prediction with graph neural networks to solve PDEs across unseen meshes and higher resolutions.

paragraphs: Graph retrieval ranks stored graphs by similarity to a query. A useful measure is the size of their largest shared subgraph, sometimes with the additional requirement that it be connected. Computing these quantities exactly is intractable, but approximate scores may be sufficient when the objective is to rank candidates.

The authors develop neural approximations for both common-edge and connected-common-subgraph measures. Their formulations use a continuous relaxation of the alignment between nodes in the two graphs. Late interaction models represent each graph separately before comparing them, supporting scalability. Early interaction models exchange information between the graphs from the input stages. A differentiable component estimates the largest connected shared structure.

Experiments on seven datasets show that the proposed late interaction models outperform other late interaction methods in both accuracy and speed. The early interaction models achieve accuracy competitive with the state of the art at substantially higher speeds. The paper thus offers alternatives for different retrieval needs while retaining a similarity objective grounded in shared graph structure.
neurips-2022-maximum-common-subgraph-gui.tldr: Neural approximations of maximum common subgraphs enable fast graph retrieval with competitive accuracy in both early and late interaction models.

paragraphs: Node perturbation learns by slightly changing neural activity, observing whether performance improves, and using that feedback to adjust weights. It is a candidate biologically plausible learning rule because learning can rely on local information and reward. This paper asks whether the approach remains stable and practical as networks become larger.

The analysis of linear networks with one hidden layer finds that learning time and performance depend only weakly on hidden-layer size. However, in the analyzed setting, a mismatch between student and teacher networks makes node perturbation unstable, unlike stochastic gradient descent. Weight diffusion drives the instability: weights eventually grow very large. Normalizing weights can suppress this behavior, but introduces bias into the learning rule.

Numerical studies of deep nonlinear networks on motor control and image classification show a similar instability, along with weaker evidence of the favorable scaling behavior. The results separate two questions that might otherwise be conflated: weak dependence on network size does not ensure stable learning. Weight normalization offers a remedy with an explicit tradeoff rather than removing the problem without consequence.
neurips-2022-on-the-stability-and-scalab.tldr: Node perturbation can scale favorably with network width, but model mismatch causes instability that weight normalization suppresses at the cost of bias.

paragraphs: Human peripheral vision processes visual information differently depending on its distance from the center of gaze. This paper uses that spatial organization as inspiration for a visual recognition network. Its central question is whether a Transformer can learn useful distinctions between peripheral regions when deciding how to combine image information.

The proposed Peripheral Vision Transformer, or PerViT, adds peripheral position encoding to multi-head self-attention layers. This encoding lets the model learn a partition of the visual field into diverse peripheral regions from training data. The approach places the biological inspiration inside the attention mechanism, where spatial organization can influence how the network processes visual features.

Evaluation on ImageNet-1K reports image-classification improvements over baselines across different model sizes. The authors also inspect the model's internal workings and find visual processing patterns resembling aspects of human vision. These analyses support the proposed peripheral organization as useful for machine perception. The reported resemblance concerns learned processing behavior, while the classification comparisons provide the direct evidence of improved task performance.
neurips-2022-peripheral-vision-transform.tldr: PerViT adds learnable peripheral spatial organization to Transformer attention, improving ImageNet classification across model sizes.

paragraphs: Many vision tasks need a graph connecting images even though no graph is supplied. A common construction treats images as nodes and uses feature similarity to determine connections. The difficulty is that noisy image features can distort pairwise similarities, producing unreliable edges and therefore an unreliable graph.

This paper reframes edge creation as a statistical decision. Treating each node's feature vector as an independent sample, a similarity-based decision about one pair becomes a single statistical test. The proposed method draws and integrates multiple samples through multiple tests, building a more reliable similarity measure from the combined evidence. An efficient matrix formulation implements the approach as B-Attention.

The authors support the robustness of this multiple-test approach both theoretically and through experiments on clustering and person re-identification benchmarks. The practical contribution is a way to improve the connectivity being learned from features, rather than assuming those features already define dependable edges. Pooling statistical evidence targets the sensitivity of individual pairwise comparisons to noise.
neurips-2022-robust-graph-structure-lear.tldr: B-Attention combines multiple statistical tests to construct more reliable graph connections from noisy image features.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks a policy that performs well despite uncertainty about the environment. Its objective considers the worst-performing model within a specified uncertainty set. This is relevant when a simulator is imperfect, system dynamics change, or disturbances affect behavior. The paper asks how to learn such a policy using only previously collected data.

The proposed Robust Fitted Q-Iteration algorithm, RFQI, addresses this offline setting. Robustness introduces an inner minimization over possible models into the Bellman operator used for learning. With a fixed dataset, that extra optimization creates difficulties involving data collection, optimization over models, and unbiased estimation. The authors develop a systematic approach to handle these challenges together.

Under standard assumptions, the paper proves that RFQI learns a near-optimal robust policy. Benchmark experiments also show superior performance. The guarantee concerns robustness within the modeled uncertainty set and is conditional on the assumptions, so the stated theoretical result is more specific than unconditional protection against any environmental change. Its significance is obtaining a principled robust-learning procedure from offline data alone.
neurips-2022-robust-reinforcement-learni.tldr: RFQI learns robust policies from offline data and has a near-optimality guarantee under standard assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how features change during gradient-flow training in infinite-width neural networks. Rather than tracking every neuron individually, it describes training through deterministic kernels: inner products of hidden activations and gradients across layers and pairs of times. Together, these quantities determine activation distributions, neural tangent kernel evolution, and predictions.

The authors derive a self-consistent dynamical field theory that recovers an existing infinite-width feature-learning process. For deep linear networks, the kernels satisfy algebraic matrix equations. For nonlinear networks, an alternating sampling procedure solves for them self-consistently, so the quantities describing different aspects of network activity agree with the dynamics they collectively generate.

Comparisons show that the static neural tangent kernel approximation, gradient independence assumption, and leading-order perturbation theory can each fail in regimes where the self-consistent solution remains accurate. Additional CNN experiments on a CIFAR classification task find preserved loss and kernel dynamics across widths when feature-learning strength is fixed. These results support tracking evolving kernels when simpler approximations no longer capture training behavior.
neurips-2022-self-consistent-dynamical-f.tldr: A self-consistent field theory tracks evolving kernels during wide-network feature learning, remaining accurate in regimes where simpler approximations fail.

paragraphs: Object rearrangement can involve producing an acceptable layout rather than reaching one precisely specified arrangement. This paper learns that goal from examples of desirable configurations. The setting avoids requiring a handcrafted reward that describes all acceptable layouts or expert trajectories demonstrating how to reach them from shuffled starting states.

TarGF uses score matching to learn a target gradient field. For each object, the field supplies a direction that would increase the likelihood of the configuration under the target distribution. The authors connect this signal to two control approaches. Model-based planning turns it into reference control for a distributed path planner. Model-free reinforcement learning uses estimated likelihood changes as rewards and the field's suggested actions in residual policy learning.

Experiments on ball and room rearrangement report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in final-layout quality, control efficiency, and scalability. The contribution is a reusable connection between examples of desired outcomes and action guidance. Its target is a distribution of acceptable arrangements, allowing the learned signal to guide rearrangement without an explicitly specified final configuration.
neurips-2022-targf-learning-target-gradi.tldr: TarGF learns movement guidance from examples of desirable layouts and uses it for planning or reinforcement learning without explicit goal configurations.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to imitate a larger teacher. Yet increasing the teacher's capacity does not necessarily improve the student. This paper attributes that phenomenon to undistillable classes: categories for which the teacher's knowledge is not successfully learned by the student through distillation.

The authors find that overall accuracy can improve while performance on these particular classes deteriorates. They establish the widespread presence of such classes in state-of-the-art distillation methods and show a correlation with the capacity gap between teacher and student. This class-level view exposes a failure that aggregate accuracy can conceal and helps explain why a stronger teacher may not yield a stronger student.

The proposed Teach Less Learn More framework identifies and discards undistillable classes during training. Evaluations cover multiple datasets and different network architectures, and the method exceeds competitive state-of-the-art techniques in all reported settings. The findings support selective teaching as a way to improve distillation when some parts of the teacher's knowledge are poorly matched to the student's capacity.
neurips-2022-teach-less-learn-more-on-th.tldr: Teach Less Learn More improves distillation by identifying and discarding classes whose teacher knowledge the student cannot effectively absorb.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization can benefit from previous tuning experiments, but existing learned optimizers are often restricted to experiments with the same hyperparameters. OptFormer introduces a text-based Transformer framework intended to learn across more varied tuning records. Its unified interface jointly learns how to propose configurations and how to predict their outcomes.

The framework trains on extensive real-world tuning data, such as Google's Vizier database. Experiments show that it can imitate at least seven distinct hyperparameter optimization algorithms within one model. Its estimates of uncertainty about objective values can further improve the imitated optimization behavior, connecting prediction with the choice of what to evaluate.

Compared with a Gaussian process, OptFormer learns a robust prior over hyperparameter response functions and provides more accurate, better-calibrated predictions in the reported experiments. These findings demonstrate useful shared learning across optimization behaviors and tasks. The paper frames this as progress toward a general Transformer-based optimizer, with a universal interface already provided and broader optimizer capability remaining a direction for future extensions.
neurips-2022-towards-learning-universal-.tldr: OptFormer learns hyperparameter proposals and outcome predictions from diverse tuning histories, imitating multiple optimizers within a text-based Transformer framework.

paragraphs: An invariant representation stays the same under a chosen transformation, while an equivariant representation changes in a corresponding, structured way. This paper brings both ideas into unsupervised learning. It asks how a network can preserve transformation-independent information while still retaining what is needed to reconstruct the original input.

The proposed encoder-decoder separates its latent representation into an invariant component and a component describing a group action. The network learns to predict the action needed to align the input and reconstructed output. Reconstruction therefore requires both a representation that ignores the relevant pose change and information that restores the appropriate pose.

The authors derive necessary conditions on the equivariant encoder and give a construction valid for any group, whether discrete or continuous. They explicitly describe rotations, translations, and permutations. Experiments across diverse data types and architectures test the method's validity and robustness. The contribution is a general construction for combining invariance with reconstruction, where transformation information has a distinct role rather than being lost when an invariant representation is learned.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-learning-of-gr.tldr: An unsupervised encoder-decoder separates invariant content from a learned group action, allowing reconstruction while respecting transformation structure.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm chooses actions while learning from limited reward feedback. This paper studies the additional difficulty of requiring global differential privacy. It proves minimax and problem-dependent regret lower bounds for stochastic and linear bandits, quantifying unavoidable losses from learning under both partial information and a privacy constraint.

The bounds suggest two regimes. With strong privacy, corresponding to a small privacy budget, difficulty reflects a coupled effect of privacy and incomplete knowledge of rewards. With weaker privacy, the private problem is no harder in the characterized sense than its non-private counterpart. This distinction explains why privacy's learning cost depends on the regime.

For stochastic bandits, the authors give a framework combining Laplace noise, adaptive episodes for each arm, and private statistics computed only from the latest episode's rewards. It produces private variants of UCB and KL-UCB. The resulting AdaP-KLUCB algorithm satisfies global differential privacy and matches the problem-dependent regret lower bound up to multiplicative constants, connecting the hardness analysis to an algorithm with a correspondingly strong guarantee.
neurips-2022-when-privacy-meets-partial-.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy-dependent bandit difficulty and introduces a globally private algorithm matching the problem-dependent regret lower bound up to constants.
